claim: Two monkeys (Macaca mulatta; monkeys H and K) were trained to perform rule-guided center-out reaches with sequential cueing.
source: Two monkeys (Macaca mulatta; monkeys H and K) were trained to perform rule-guided center-out reaches with sequential cueing (Figure 1; see also our human behavioral study Suriya-Arunroj and Gail, 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text describing the experimental subjects and task.

claim: In instructed trials, monkeys made fewer errors when the rule-cue followed the high-prior direction.
source: In instructed trials, monkeys made fewer errors when the rule-cue followed the high-prior direction and more errors when it was against the prior (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and statistical analysis (t-statistic = −21.26, p<0.001; GLMM).

claim: Monkeys made more errors when the rule-cue was against the prior.
source: In instructed trials, monkeys made fewer errors when the rule-cue followed the high-prior direction and more errors when it was against the prior (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2a and statistical analysis (against: t-statistic = 53.92, p<0.001; GLMM).

claim: Monkeys had slower responses in against trials.
source: Also, the monkeys had slower responses in against trials and faster responses in follow trials (against: t-statistic = 24.02, p<0.001; follow: t-statistic = −76.31, p<0.001; GLMM; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by reaction time data shown in Figure 2b and statistical analysis.

claim: Monkeys had faster responses in follow trials.
source: Also, the monkeys had slower responses in against trials and faster responses in follow trials (against: t-statistic = 24.02, p<0.001; follow: t-statistic = −76.31, p<0.001; GLMM; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by reaction time data shown in Figure 2b and statistical analysis.

claim: In free-choice trials, monkeys showed a choice bias toward the reach direction pre-cued with higher prior.
source: In free-choice trials, monkeys showed a choice bias toward the reach direction pre-cued with higher prior and the bias gradually increased with prior (t-statistic = 8.17, p<0.001; GLMM; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by choice probability data shown in Figure 2c and statistical analysis.

claim: The choice bias gradually increased with prior.
source: In free-choice trials, monkeys showed a choice bias toward the reach direction pre-cued with higher prior and the bias gradually increased with prior (t-statistic = 8.17, p<0.001; GLMM; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by choice probability data shown in Figure 2c and statistical analysis.

claim: At the strongest prior level, monkeys almost exclusively (89%) chose the high-prior direction.
source: At the strongest prior level, monkeys almost exclusively (89%) chose the high-prior direction.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the choice probability data.

claim: Choice RTs were slower in against trials.
source: Like in instructed reaches, choice RTs were slower in against trials (t-statistic = 14.61, p<0.001; GLMM) and faster in follow trials (t-statistic = −42.76, p<0.001; GLMM) and the effect increased with strength of prior (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by reaction time data in free-choice trials shown in Figure 2d and statistical analysis.

claim: Choice RTs were faster in follow trials.
source: Like in instructed reaches, choice RTs were slower in against trials (t-statistic = 14.61, p<0.001; GLMM) and faster in follow trials (t-statistic = −42.76, p<0.001; GLMM) and the effect increased with strength of prior (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by reaction time data in free-choice trials shown in Figure 2d and statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of prior on choice RTs increased with strength of prior.
source: Like in instructed reaches, choice RTs were slower in against trials (t-statistic = 14.61, p<0.001; GLMM) and faster in follow trials (t-statistic = −42.76, p<0.001; GLMM) and the effect increased with strength of prior (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the pattern of reaction time data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Monkey K achieved 96% correct reaches in full-prior trials when trials were not aborted due to fixation breaks.
source: Monkey K achieved very good performance with 96% correct reaches in full-prior trials when trials were not aborted due to fixation breaks.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral performance data for monkey K.

claim: Monkey H achieved 94% correct reaches in full-prior trials.
source: Monkey H also understood the task very well with 94% correct reaches in full-prior trials, but high failure rate when fixation was imposed during the pre-cue.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral performance data for monkey H.

claim: 561 well-isolated units were recorded from PMd of both monkeys (H: 238, K: 323).
source: We recorded extracellular single-unit spiking activities from 561 well-isolated units in PMd of both monkeys (H: 238, K: 323) and 517 units in PRR (H: 248, K: 269), while animals performed the task.
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of recorded neurons.

claim: 517 units were recorded from PRR of both monkeys (H: 248, K: 269).
source: We recorded extracellular single-unit spiking activities from 561 well-isolated units in PMd of both monkeys (H: 238, K: 323) and 517 units in PRR (H: 248, K: 269), while animals performed the task.
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of recorded neurons.

claim: 53% of PMd units (297/561) were spatially selective for the motor goal during planning.
source: 53% of PMd (297/561) and 50% of PRR (261/517) units were spatially selective for the motor goal during planning (motor-goal neurons; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and were used for all following analyses.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the spatial selectivity analysis.

claim: 50% of PRR units (261/517) were spatially selective for the motor goal during planning.
source: 53% of PMd (297/561) and 50% of PRR (261/517) units were spatially selective for the motor goal during planning (motor-goal neurons; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and were used for all following analyses.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the spatial selectivity analysis.

claim: 60% of motor-goal neurons in PMd showed either increased or decreased planning-period responses based on prior direction.
source: After receiving prior information from the pre-cue, the majority of the motor-goal neurons in PMd (60%) and particularly in PRR (76%) either showed increased planning-period responses when the higher prior coincided with the maximal responsive direction (PDmax) of the neuron (Figure 3a-left) or decreased when prior coincided with the opposite direction (OD) of the neuron (Figure 3a-right), but not both.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of neuronal modulation patterns.

claim: 76% of motor-goal neurons in PRR showed either increased or decreased planning-period responses based on prior direction.
source: After receiving prior information from the pre-cue, the majority of the motor-goal neurons in PMd (60%) and particularly in PRR (76%) either showed increased planning-period responses when the higher prior coincided with the maximal responsive direction (PDmax) of the neuron (Figure 3a-left) or decreased when prior coincided with the opposite direction (OD) of the neuron (Figure 3a-right), but not both.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of neuronal modulation patterns.

claim: Most motor-goal neurons showed either upregulation or downregulation, but rarely both.
source: When plotting prior modulations at PDmax against OD, most motor-goal neurons coalesced along the axes and not along the unity line (Figure 3b), suggesting that motor-goal neurons mostly showed either upregulation or downregulation, and rarely both.
evidence: This is supported by the scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The distribution of relative modulation strengths in both brain areas is bimodal.
source: The means the example neurons in Figure 3a do not represent the opposite ends of a continuous distribution, but rather two distinct neuron classes, further confirmed from the bimodal distribution of relative modulation strengths in both brain areas (Hartigans dip test of unimodality; PMd: p < 0.005; PRR: p < 0.001; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Hartigans dip test) and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: PMd and PRR grand-average populations showed higher activity when the higher prior was toward PD (PDmax: PMd: p<0.001; PRR: p<0.001).
source: PMd and PRR grand-average populations showed higher activity when the higher prior was toward PD (PDmax: PMd: p<0.001; PRR: p<0.001) and lower activity with increasing prior away from PD (OD: PMd: p<0.001; PRR: p<0.001; GLMM; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by population-level analysis shown in Figure 4b and statistical testing.

claim: PMd and PRR grand-average populations showed lower activity with increasing prior away from PD (OD: PMd: p<0.001; PRR: p<0.001).
source: PMd and PRR grand-average populations showed higher activity when the higher prior was toward PD (PDmax: PMd: p<0.001; PRR: p<0.001) and lower activity with increasing prior away from PD (OD: PMd: p<0.001; PRR: p<0.001; GLMM; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by population-level analysis shown in Figure 4b and statistical testing.

claim: The graded motor-goal encoding in the population mirrored the graded behavioral bias.
source: The graded motor-goal encoding in the population (Figure 4b) mirrored the graded behavioral bias (Figure 2), even respecting idiosyncratic non-linear pattern of choice biases in each monkey (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of neural and behavioral data across Figures 2, 4b, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upregulating neurons in PMd showed significant modulation at PDmax (p<0.001) but not at OD (p>0.5) or Orth (p>0.5).
source: The neuronal subclasses contribute to either the up- or downregulating graded modulation, in accordance with their class definition (PMd-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.5; Orth: p>0.5; PRR-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.05; Orth: p>0.05; PMd-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; PRR-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; GLMM; Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (GLMM) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Upregulating neurons in PRR showed significant modulation at PDmax (p<0.001) but not at OD (p>0.05) or Orth (p>0.05).
source: The neuronal subclasses contribute to either the up- or downregulating graded modulation, in accordance with their class definition (PMd-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.5; Orth: p>0.5; PRR-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.05; Orth: p>0.05; PMd-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; PRR-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; GLMM; Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (GLMM) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Downregulating neurons in PMd showed significant modulation at OD (p<0.001) but not at PDmax (p>0.05) or Orth (p>0.05).
source: The neuronal subclasses contribute to either the up- or downregulating graded modulation, in accordance with their class definition (PMd-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.5; Orth: p>0.5; PRR-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.05; Orth: p>0.05; PMd-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; PRR-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; GLMM; Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (GLMM) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Downregulating neurons in PRR showed significant modulation at OD (p<0.001) but not at PDmax (p>0.05) or Orth (p>0.05).
source: The neuronal subclasses contribute to either the up- or downregulating graded modulation, in accordance with their class definition (PMd-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.5; Orth: p>0.5; PRR-UR: PDmax: p<0.001; OD: p>0.05; Orth: p>0.05; PMd-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; PRR-DR: PDmax: p>0.05; OD: p<0.001; Orth: p>0.05; GLMM; Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (GLMM) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: In zero-prior trials, neuronal population responses were higher when the two potential reach goals matched their PDmax and OD than when they were orthogonal to it (Orth).
source: In zero-prior trials, when both reach goals were equipotent, neuronal population responses were higher when the two potential reach goals matched their PDmax and OD than when they were orthogonal to it (Orth).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of responses at different directions in zero-prior conditions.

claim: Downregulating neurons in PMd showed higher responses at PDmax compared to Orth in zero-prior trials (pcorr <0.001).
source: This response was evident in downregulating neurons (zero-prior; PMd-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; PRR-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test; Figure 4c–d), whereas upregulating neurons, if at all, showed slightly higher activities when potential reach goals were orthogonal to their PDmax (zero-prior; PMd-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; Orth-OD: pcorr <0.01; PRR-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.05; Bonferroni-corrected t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Downregulating neurons in PMd showed higher responses at OD compared to Orth in zero-prior trials (pcorr <0.001).
source: This response was evident in downregulating neurons (zero-prior; PMd-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; PRR-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test; Figure 4c–d), whereas upregulating neurons, if at all, showed slightly higher activities when potential reach goals were orthogonal to their PDmax (zero-prior; PMd-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; Orth-OD: pcorr <0.01; PRR-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.05; Bonferroni-corrected t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Downregulating neurons in PRR showed higher responses at PDmax compared to Orth in zero-prior trials (pcorr <0.001).
source: This response was evident in downregulating neurons (zero-prior; PMd-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; PRR-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test; Figure 4c–d), whereas upregulating neurons, if at all, showed slightly higher activities when potential reach goals were orthogonal to their PDmax (zero-prior; PMd-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; Orth-OD: pcorr <0.01; PRR-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.05; Bonferroni-corrected t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Downregulating neurons in PRR showed higher responses at OD compared to Orth in zero-prior trials (pcorr <0.001).
source: This response was evident in downregulating neurons (zero-prior; PMd-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; PRR-DR: PDmax-Orth: pcorr <0.001; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test; Figure 4c–d), whereas upregulating neurons, if at all, showed slightly higher activities when potential reach goals were orthogonal to their PDmax (zero-prior; PMd-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; Orth-OD: pcorr <0.01; PRR-UR: Orth-PDmax: pcorr >0.05; OD-Orth: pcorr <0.05; Bonferroni-corrected t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test) and shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: No significant modulation was observed at orthogonal directions in PMd (p>0.1).
source: No significant modulation was observed at orthogonal directions (PMd: p>0.1; PRR: p>0.1; GLMM; Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (GLMM) and shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: No significant modulation was observed at orthogonal directions in PRR (p>0.1).
source: No significant modulation was observed at orthogonal directions (PMd: p>0.1; PRR: p>0.1; GLMM; Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (GLMM) and shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: When the maximally strong prior was directed away from neurons' PD, the response strength of DR neurons in PMd dropped below the level of Orth activities (full-prior; PMd-DR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001).
source: When the maximally strong prior was directed away from neurons' PD, the response strength of DR neurons even dropped below the level of Orth activities (full-prior; PMd-DR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001; PRR-DR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test) and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: When the maximally strong prior was directed away from neurons' PD, the response strength of DR neurons in PRR dropped below the level of Orth activities (full-prior; PRR-DR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001).
source: When the maximally strong prior was directed away from neurons' PD, the response strength of DR neurons even dropped below the level of Orth activities (full-prior; PMd-DR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001; PRR-DR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test) and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: UR neurons in PMd showed OD activity levels that were overall below the level of Orth activities and the difference became strongest at full-prior level (full-prior; PMd-UR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001).
source: UR neurons showed OD activity levels that were overall below the level of Orth activities and the difference became strongest at full-prior level (full-prior; PMd-UR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001; PRR-UR: OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test).

claim: UR neurons in PRR showed OD activity levels that were overall below the level of Orth activities and the difference became strongest at full-prior level (full-prior; PRR-UR: OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001).
source: UR neurons showed OD activity levels that were overall below the level of Orth activities and the difference became strongest at full-prior level (full-prior; PMd-UR: Orth-OD: pcorr <0.001; PRR-UR: OD-Orth: pcorr <0.001; Bonferroni-corrected t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected t-test).

claim: Prior-induced modulation emerges early during pre-cue presentation then lasts until or beyond commitment to an action in both UR- and DR-neurons of PMd and PRR.
source: Population-average spike density functions show that prior-induced modulation emerges early during pre-cue presentation then lasts until or beyond commitment to an action in both UR- and DR-neurons of PMd and PRR (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in the temporal dynamics of population responses in Figure 5a.

claim: MVTs qualitatively reflected the prior-dependent RT patterns in instructed and free-choice trials.
source: MVTs qualitatively reflected the prior-dependent RT patterns in instructed and free-choice trials (Figure 5b–c), being faster for follow versus against trials and scaling with strength of prior.
evidence: This is shown by comparison of MVTs and RTs in Figure 5b-c.

claim: MVTs were faster for follow versus against trials.
source: MVTs qualitatively reflected the prior-dependent RT patterns in instructed and free-choice trials (Figure 5b–c), being faster for follow versus against trials and scaling with strength of prior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b-c.

claim: MVTs scaled with strength of prior.
source: MVTs qualitatively reflected the prior-dependent RT patterns in instructed and free-choice trials (Figure 5b–c), being faster for follow versus against trials and scaling with strength of prior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b-c.

claim: The modulation of neural latencies by prior was larger than the modulation of behavioral latencies.
source: Quantitatively, the modulation of neural latencies by prior was, however, larger than the modulation of behavioral latencies.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of neural and behavioral latency data.

claim: Latency differences between brain areas are most evident in DR neurons, with PMd showing earlier MVTs than PRR.
source: Latency differences between brain areas are most evident in DR neurons, with PMd showing earlier MVTs than PRR (pairwise permutation test; Figure 5c-left).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (pairwise permutation test) and shown in Figure 5c-left.

claim: UR neurons in both PMd and PRR showed comparable MVTs.
source: In contrast, UR neurons in both PMd and PRR showed comparable MVTs (Figure 5c-right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c-right.

claim: DR neurons signaled the selected movement earlier than UR neurons in PMd.
source: DR neurons signaled the selected movement earlier than UR neurons in PMd whereas the difference between DR and UR subclasses in PRR was not significant (Supp. Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The difference between DR and UR subclasses in PRR was not significant.
source: DR neurons signaled the selected movement earlier than UR neurons in PMd whereas the difference between DR and UR subclasses in PRR was not significant (Supp. Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: MVTs were reached earliest in DR neurons of PMd (Free-choice: against: 210 [193–227; 90% bootstrapped CI] ms; no-prior: 126 [103-172] ms; follow:72 [53-94] ms).
source: Despite slight variations in different task conditions, MVTs were overall reached the earliest in DR neurons of PMd (Free-choice: against: 210 [193–227; 90% bootstrapped CI] ms; no-prior: 126 [103-172] ms; follow:72 [53-94] ms), then in UR neurons of PMd and DR neurons of PRR, and finally in UR neurons of PRR (Free-choice: against: 261 [228-318] ms; no-prior: 204 [176-240] ms; follow:160 [145-190] ms; Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MVT analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: MVTs were reached latest in UR neurons of PRR (Free-choice: against: 261 [228-318] ms; no-prior: 204 [176-240] ms; follow:160 [145-190] ms).
source: Despite slight variations in different task conditions, MVTs were overall reached the earliest in DR neurons of PMd (Free-choice: against: 210 [193–227; 90% bootstrapped CI] ms; no-prior: 126 [103-172] ms; follow:72 [53-94] ms), then in UR neurons of PMd and DR neurons of PRR, and finally in UR neurons of PRR (Free-choice: against: 261 [228-318] ms; no-prior: 204 [176-240] ms; follow:160 [145-190] ms; Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MVT analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The latest subclass, PRR-UR neurons, reached MVTs at ~50–100 ms after the earliest subclass, PMd-DR neurons.
source: The latest subclass, PRR-UR neurons, reached MVTs at ~50–100 ms after the earliest subclass, PMd-DR neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the MVT data comparing the earliest and latest subclasses.

claim: PTs mostly matched movement onset or lagged behind.
source: PTs mostly matched movement onset or lagged behind, but overall followed the same ranking pattern as MVTs, hence showed converging results on latency differences between neuron classes and brain areas (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: PTs followed the same ranking pattern as MVTs.
source: PTs mostly matched movement onset or lagged behind, but overall followed the same ranking pattern as MVTs, hence showed converging results on latency differences between neuron classes and brain areas (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Neuronal signatures of action selection manifested earlier in PMd than in PRR.
source: In summary, in the transition from encoding of prior-modulated motor goals to actual movement execution, neuronal signatures of action selection manifested earlier in PMd than in PRR and the leading role of PMd is driven by the DR neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the MVT and PT analyses.

claim: The leading role of PMd in action selection is driven by the DR neurons.
source: In summary, in the transition from encoding of prior-modulated motor goals to actual movement execution, neuronal signatures of action selection manifested earlier in PMd than in PRR and the leading role of PMd is driven by the DR neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the MVT and PT analyses.

claim: Action priors can promote preliminary action planning and influence choices.
source: Prior expectations of movement instructions can promote preliminary action planning and influence choices.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: Action priors induced graded free-choice biases and graded frontoparietal motor-goal activity.
source: Action priors induced graded free-choice biases and graded frontoparietal motor-goal activity, complementarily in two subclasses of neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Down-regulating neurons co-encoded both possible goals.
source: Down-regulating neurons co-encoded both possible goals and decreased opposite-to-preferred responses with decreasing prior, possibly supporting a process of choice by elimination.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Down-regulating neurons decreased opposite-to-preferred responses with decreasing prior.
source: Down-regulating neurons co-encoded both possible goals and decreased opposite-to-preferred responses with decreasing prior, possibly supporting a process of choice by elimination.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Down-regulating neurons possibly support a process of choice by elimination.
source: Down-regulating neurons co-encoded both possible goals and decreased opposite-to-preferred responses with decreasing prior, possibly supporting a process of choice by elimination.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Up-regulating neurons showed increased preferred-direction responses with increasing prior.
source: Up-regulating neurons showed increased preferred-direction responses with increasing prior, likely supporting a process of computing net likelihood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Up-regulating neurons likely support a process of computing net likelihood.
source: Up-regulating neurons showed increased preferred-direction responses with increasing prior, likely supporting a process of computing net likelihood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Action-selection signals emerged earliest in down-regulating neurons of premotor cortex.
source: Action-selection signals emerged earliest in down-regulating neurons of premotor cortex, arguing for an initiation of selection in the frontal lobe.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The earliest emergence of action-selection signals in down-regulating neurons of premotor cortex argues for an initiation of selection in the frontal lobe.
source: Action-selection signals emerged earliest in down-regulating neurons of premotor cortex, arguing for an initiation of selection in the frontal lobe.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Prior probabilities allow us to prepare the action mostly likely to become relevant, thereby helping us economize reaction times and improve accuracy.
source: These kinds of prior probabilities allow us to prepare the action mostly likely to become relevant, thereby helping us economize reaction times and improve accuracy (Dorris and Munoz, 1998; Basso and Wurtz, 1998; Gold et al., 2008; Suriya-Arunroj and Gail, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: We need to keep track of available action alternatives, the choice set, before commitment to a choice.
source: At the same time, we need to keep track of available action alternatives, the choice set, before commitment to a choice, for example potential reach goals in action-selection tasks (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005; Klaes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When action and reward probabilities are confounded, it is unclear whether the behavioral benefit of priors results from the possibility for action planning or from higher motivation elicited by events that provide higher expected reward.
source: When action and reward probabilities are confounded, it is unclear whether the behavioral benefit of priors results from the possibility for action planning thanks to higher predictability of future events or from higher motivation elicited by events that provide higher expected reward, defined as the product of reward amount and probability (Neumann Von et al., 1944; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the ambiguity in interpreting prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Choice biases due to reward-related priors have been investigated.
source: Choice biases due to reward-related priors have been investigated (Sugrue, 2004; Yang and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Much less is known about how action-related priors bias choice when expected reward is symmetric between both options.
source: Much less is known about how action-related priors bias choice (Funahashi, 2017) when expected reward is symmetric between both options ('free' choice).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: In human subjects, action priors bias reward-symmetric free choices, whereas pure reward priors do not.
source: We recently demonstrated in human subjects that action priors bias reward-symmetric free choices, whereas pure reward priors do not (Suriya-Arunroj and Gail, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Sensorimotor decisions are achieved through competition between action plans.
source: Based on the idea that sensorimotor decisions are achieved through competition between action plans (Gallivan et al., 2018; Gallivan et al., 2015; Cisek, 2012; Cisek, 2007; Klaes et al., 2012), we postulated that action priors induce behavioral bias by establishing an imbalanced action planning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Action priors induce behavioral bias by establishing an imbalanced action planning.
source: Based on the idea that sensorimotor decisions are achieved through competition between action plans (Gallivan et al., 2018; Gallivan et al., 2015; Cisek, 2012; Cisek, 2007; Klaes et al., 2012), we postulated that action priors induce behavioral bias by establishing an imbalanced action planning.
evidence: This is a hypothesis postulated by the authors based on previous literature.

claim: In reach tasks, reach plans are reflected by the encoding of spatially defined reach endpoints ('goals') in reach-planning brain areas.
source: In reach tasks, reach plans are reflected by the encoding of spatially defined reach endpoints ('goals') in reach-planning brain areas.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sustained neural co-encoding of potential motor-goal locations during planning could serve maintenance of the choice set in working memory.
source: As previously observed in tasks in which multiple reach goals are narrowed down to two alternatives in each trial, sustained neural co-encoding of potential motor-goal locations during planning (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005; Klaes et al., 2011), could serve maintenance of the choice set in working memory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous observations, supported by citations.

claim: Previously reported potential-response cells were activated whenever one of two equipotent reach goals overlapped with the preferred direction of the neuron.
source: At single-neuron level, previously reported potential-response cells were activated whenever one of two equipotent reach goals overlapped with the preferred direction of the neuron (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005; Klaes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mutual roles of frontal versus parietal sensorimotor structures in action planning and decision making are still inconclusive.
source: The mutual roles of frontal versus parietal sensorimotor structures in action planning and decision making are still inconclusive (Westendorff et al., 2010; Hanks et al., 2015; Siegel et al., 2015; Brown et al., 2007; Connolly et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Simultaneous action-selection signals in both areas would suggest common input about action-selection outcome from other brain structures or that both areas converge onto the same solution in consensus.
source: Simultaneous action-selection signals in both areas would suggest common input about action-selection outcome from other brain structures or that both areas converge onto the same solution in consensus.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what simultaneous signals would imply.

claim: Latency differences of selection signals between areas could be indicative of a processing hierarchy during reach selection.
source: Instead, latency differences of selection signals between areas could be indicative of a processing hierarchy during reach selection.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what latency differences would imply.

claim: The task design dissociates motor goals from visual stimulus locations.
source: One idea of the design is that motor goals are dissociated from visual stimulus locations (Crammond and Kalaska, 1994; Gail et al., 2009; Westendorff et al., 2010), which allows investigating motor-goal encoding independent of visual target encoding, which is important in visuomotor brain areas (Boussaoud and Wise, 1993; di Pellegrino and Wise, 1993; Crammond and Kalaska, 1994; Gail and Andersen, 2006; Kuang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the task design rationale, supported by citations.

claim: The task design encouraged sustained preliminary planning of two alternative movements.
source: Second, the task design encouraged sustained preliminary planning of two alternative movements, because the two out of four locations of the potential reach-goals varied across trials and the final instruction was provided only after a variable delay (planning period).
evidence: This is a description of the task design rationale.

claim: The task discouraged premature commitment to a choice before the go cue.
source: The task discouraged premature commitment to a choice before the go cue because free-choice trials were rare and the trial type, instructed or free-choice, was revealed only at the time of the go cue (Klaes et al., 2011; Klaes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the task design rationale, supported by citations.

claim: The use of four reach directions allowed estimating the spatial response properties of neurons beyond the two potential motor-goal directions.
source: Third, different to binary choice tasks, the use of four reach directions allowed estimating the spatial response properties of neurons beyond the two potential motor-goal directions.
evidence: This is a description of the task design rationale.

claim: Behavioral asymmetries were observed despite the symmetric expected reward at the moment of commitment.
source: These behavioral asymmetries were observed despite the symmetric expected reward at the moment of commitment, that is without a value-associated advantage of either option.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the behavioral results.

claim: Both monkeys understood the task.
source: Both monkeys understood the task and showed near-perfect performance in full-prior trials (96% and 94%; monkeys K and H).
evidence: This is supported by the high performance rates in full-prior trials.

claim: There was a slight effect of previous trials on the accuracy of the following instructed trials as well as the choice of the following free-choice trials.
source: We did observe slight effect of previous trials on the accuracy of the following instructed trials as well as the choice of the following free-choice trials (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, though data are not shown.

claim: The effect of previous trials did not support win-stay/lose-shift strategy but rather suggested that monkeys sometimes corrected their behavior after an error trial.
source: This effect did not support win-stay/lose-shift strategy but rather suggested that monkeys sometimes corrected their behavior after an error trial.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed effect of previous trials.

claim: Aside from stronger cue-related neuronal activities during the initial phase of pre-cue presentation in monkey H, the neuronal activity patterns of both monkeys were comparable during the rest of the trial.
source: Aside from stronger cue-related neuronal activities during the initial phase of pre-cue presentation in monkey H, the neuronal activity patterns of both monkeys were comparable during the rest of the trial.
evidence: This is a statement about the similarity of neural responses between the two monkeys.

claim: The two complementary mechanisms for encoding priors cannot be explained by ceiling or floor effects.
source: The two complementary mechanisms for encoding priors cannot be explained by ceiling or floor effects (low-firing neurons can only upregulate; high-firing neurons only downregulate), as subsampled sets of neurons with matched firing rates were equally likely to fall into either category (data not shown; but see example neurons in Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by control analyses (data not shown) and example neurons in Figure 3a.

claim: DR neurons likely correspond to potential response neurons described in a previous study.
source: The DR neurons here likely correspond to potential response neurons described in a previous study (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005); the UR neurons likely correspond to a mixture of single response and build-up neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: UR neurons likely correspond to a mixture of single response and build-up neurons.
source: The DR neurons here likely correspond to potential response neurons described in a previous study (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005); the UR neurons likely correspond to a mixture of single response and build-up neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous literature.

claim: The bimodal distribution of graded units does not result from the preselection of motor-goal neurons in the analyses.
source: We ruled out that the bimodal distribution of graded units results from the preselection of motor-goal neurons in our analyses and that excluded units would fall between the DR and UR categories and restore a unimodal distribution.
evidence: This is supported by control analyses including all recorded units.

claim: DR neurons encode both potential motor goals.
source: DR neurons encode both potential motor goals, and are also modulated by the likelihood of the less likely goal to become instructed.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the properties of DR neurons based on the data.

claim: DR neurons are modulated by the likelihood of the less likely goal to become instructed.
source: DR neurons encode both potential motor goals, and are also modulated by the likelihood of the less likely goal to become instructed.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the properties of DR neurons based on the data.

claim: DR neurons could serve as mechanism for encoding priors and choice set in parallel before commitment to a choice.
source: Hence, they could serve as mechanism for encoding priors and choice set in parallel before commitment to a choice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the function of DR neurons.

claim: DR neurons contain information about the currently valid options.
source: DR neurons contain information about the currently valid options, in our case two out of four total.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the properties of DR neurons based on the data.

claim: DR neurons 'devaluate' the less likely option proportionally to the strength of prior.
source: At the same time, they 'devaluate' the less likely option proportionally to the strength of prior.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the properties of DR neurons based on the data.

claim: DR neurons could be a way of implementing choice by elimination strategies.
source: This could be a way of implementing choice by elimination strategies (Tversky, 1972), in which choice sets are reduced if factors rule out one option.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the function of DR neurons, supported by citation.

claim: UR neurons represent relative likelihood of choice toward their PD compared to other alternatives.
source: Conversely, UR neurons represent relative likelihood of choice toward their PD compared to other alternatives (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005) and might contribute to the encoding of decision variables (Ratcliff et al., 2016; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the function of UR neurons, supported by citations.

claim: UR neurons might contribute to the encoding of decision variables.
source: Conversely, UR neurons represent relative likelihood of choice toward their PD compared to other alternatives (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005) and might contribute to the encoding of decision variables (Ratcliff et al., 2016; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the function of UR neurons, supported by citations.

claim: The question whether our brain encodes dual movement goals during decision is currently still under active discussion and investigations.
source: The question whether our brain encodes dual movement goals during decision is currently still under active discussion and investigations (Gallivan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citation.

claim: Dekleva et al. (2018) recently argued against dual motor representation in zero-prior two-target trials.
source: Dekleva et al. (2018) recently argued against dual motor representation in zero-prior two-target trials, based on the observation that monkeys showed alternating single-target selection in such trials in their experiment.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from another study, supported by citation.

claim: Dual motor-goal encoding observed in this study is not explained by trial-averaging.
source: First, we observed dual motor-goal encoding which is not explained by trial-averaging (ROC analysis and spike-count correlations, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis and spike-count correlations shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Few human subjects in a previous study verbally reported that they employed a biased strategy, focusing on one target per trial.
source: Second, in the same task (Suriya-Arunroj and Gail, 2015), few human subjects verbally reported that they employed a biased strategy, focusing on one target per trial and seeing if the final instruction matched their initial plan (data not shown).
evidence: This is a report of verbal reports from human subjects in a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Only one monkey in Dekleva et al. showed strong evidence for single reach plan representation.
source: Similarly, only one monkey in Dekleva et al. showed strong evidence for single reach plan representation.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from another study.

claim: Single or dual motor-goal representations can be strategy-dependent.
source: We thus believe that single or dual motor-goal representations can be strategy-dependent and if subjects adopt a biased strategy, one motor-goal representation will be prominent, as we also have found previously in monkeys (Klaes et al., 2011), but not in our current data.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison with previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: The task design in Dekleva et al. did not encourage dual reach planning.
source: Third, the task design in Dekleva et al. did not encourage dual reach planning: monkeys did not have to memorize the target positions shown during the 'Target on' period as both would reappear again during the 'Go' period.
evidence: This is a critique of the task design in another study.

claim: It seems rather unlikely to find evidence for dual motor representation from the task design in Dekleva et al.
source: It seems rather unlikely to find evidence for dual motor representation from this task.
evidence: This is an inference based on critique of the task design in another study.

claim: Task designs that require animals to retain potential motor goals in memory and in which single-trial cognitive states are sparsely and randomly probed with free-choice trials are a better common ground to compare single versus dual motor representations.
source: Task designs that require animals to retain potential motor goals in memory and in which single-trial cognitive states are sparsely and randomly probed with free-choice trials are a better common ground to compare single versus dual motor representations.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future experimental design based on the authors' reasoning.

claim: Knowledge of selective inhibition can help constrain computational models of biased competition in decision making.
source: Knowledge of such selectivity can help constrain computational models of biased competition in decision making.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for computational modeling.

claim: Dynamic neural field (DNF) models consist of computational layers that represent the continuous workspace of sensory and motor parameters.
source: Dynamic neural field (DNF) models (Erlhagen and Schöner, 2002; Cisek, 2007; Klaes et al., 2012), for example, consist of computational layers that represent the continuous workspace of sensory and motor parameters, such as stimulus location or reach endpoint, and implement within-layer competition by lateral inhibitory mechanisms using center-surround excitation-inhibition (CSEI) kernels.
evidence: This is a description of DNF models, supported by citations.

claim: DNF models implement within-layer competition by lateral inhibitory mechanisms using center-surround excitation-inhibition (CSEI) kernels.
source: Dynamic neural field (DNF) models (Erlhagen and Schöner, 2002; Cisek, 2007; Klaes et al., 2012), for example, consist of computational layers that represent the continuous workspace of sensory and motor parameters, such as stimulus location or reach endpoint, and implement within-layer competition by lateral inhibitory mechanisms using center-surround excitation-inhibition (CSEI) kernels.
evidence: This is a description of DNF models, supported by citations.

claim: A previous DNF model simulation showed bimodal motor-goal representations in the zero-prior condition that, with increasing prior, showed increasing PD activities and decreasing OD activities, while Orth responses were always lowest.
source: We previously simulated biased rule-based action selection (Klaes et al., 2012) using a DNF model and showed bimodal motor-goal representations in the zero-prior condition that, with increasing prior, showed increasing PD activities and decreasing OD activities, while Orth responses were always lowest (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a description of previous modeling work, supported by citation and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The previous DNF model prediction that Orth responses were always lowest contradicts the current empirical findings.
source: The latter contradicts our current empirical findings (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a comparison between previous model predictions and current empirical findings.

claim: Anisotropic lateral inhibition could lead to strong mutual competition along the rule dimension.
source: First, DNF can be expanded with strong mutual competition selectively between association nodes with opposing rule-preference (cw or ccw) but overlapping spatial selectivity. This corresponds to an anisotropic interaction kernel, with strongest inhibition along the 'rule' dimension in the two-dimensional association field (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a proposed extension to the DNF model, illustrated in Figure 6b.

claim: The range of mutual competition along the spatial dimension could be adaptive to the task, maximized at 180° apart for center-out reach task with circular workspace.
source: Second, the range of mutual competition (i.e. the CSEI kernels) along the spatial dimension could be adaptive to the task, maximized at 180° apart for center-out reach task with circular workspace.
evidence: This is a proposed extension to the DNF model.

claim: A lack of modulation of Orth locations by priors could result from excitation and inhibition that cancel each other out at half-distance between PD and OD.
source: In this case, a lack of modulation of Orth locations by priors could result from excitation and inhibition that cancel each other out at half-distance (in direction space) between PD and OD.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the empirical findings based on the second model extension.

claim: Other decision models postulate competition between a set of discrete groups of neurons, the properties of which are defined by the specific option of the decision-making task.
source: Third, other decision models postulate competition between a set of discrete groups of neurons, the properties of which are defined by the specific option of the decision-making task (Usher and McClelland, 2004; Brown and Heathcote, 2008; Ratcliff et al., 2016; Gold and Shadlen, 2007), for example competition between cw and ccw goals in our experiment.

claim: It is important to include the implementation on a continuous coding space in the context of action-selection tasks.
source: Yet, we consider it important to include the implementation on a continuous coding space in the context of action-selection tasks (Figure 6d) to allow space-continuous motor outputs and to account for space-continuous multisensory input to posterior parietal cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' view on modeling approaches.

claim: The first explanation suggests the main competition in the upstream association field.
source: In this sense, our suggested former two explanations provide means of achieving the third. While the first explanation suggests the main competition in the upstream association field, the second explanation requires competition mostly on the motor-goal field.
evidence: This is a comparison of the proposed model extensions.
